introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2021. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown: **SECTION D: WORLD, 1919 TO THE PRESENT DATE**
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; publicités, filigranes gcerevision.com et mention manuscrite d'adresse web ignorés ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune statistique ni citation n'est avancée ; les effectifs sont donnés en ordres de grandeur prudents (« roughly nine to ten million », « about two million »).

Question 2 : l'énoncé imprimé associe « the Jihad in Futa Jallon » aux dates 1854-1864. Ces dates correspondent à la guerre sainte d'Al-Hajj Umar Tall (empire toucouleur, parti de Dinguiraye, en bordure du Fouta-Djalon), alors que le jihad du Fouta-Djalon proprement dit date d'environ 1725 (Karamoko Alfa). Le sujet est recopié tel quel ; le corrigé signale la divergence et traite le mouvement de 1854-1864, avec le jihad du Fouta-Djalon en arrière-plan. L'année de début de la guerre sainte d'Umar est donnée de façon prudente (1852 ou 1854 selon les sources).

Question 2 : détails à vérifier par un historien (siège de Médine en 1857, prise de Ségou en 1861 et de Hamdallahi en 1862, mort d'Umar en 1864, chute de Ségou face à Archinard en 1890) ; ils sont cités conformément à l'historiographie courante, mais le corrigé ne s'appuie pas sur des chiffres.

Question 7 : les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, invitation des « Immortal Seven » et acquittement des sept évêques le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre) ; le corrigé précise le choix du calendrier julien.
Question 4 : le massacre de Thiaroye (décembre 1944), les émeutes d'Accra (1948) et la conférence de Brazzaville (1944) sont cités sans bilan chiffré, le nombre exact de victimes étant discuté.

Question 5 : exemples de coups d'État (Togo 1963, Ghana 1966, Nigeria 1966, Ouganda 1971, Éthiopie 1974, Mali 2020) cités sans chiffres ; la formule « very many people were killed » remplace volontairement tout bilan sous Amin, très discuté.

Question 12 : la liste des suspensions et départs (Nigeria 1995, Fidji, Zimbabwe 2003, Gambie 2013 puis retour 2018) et l'adhésion du Cameroun en 1995 sont citées de mémoire historique ; aucun chiffre financier n'est avancé.

Questions à thème régional : les noms de thèmes sont qualifiés (par exemple `military coups in africa`, `refugee crisis in africa`, `league of nations`) pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone ; à reverifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The ineffectiveness of Collective Security was largely due to the structural lapses of the League of Nations in the 1930s. Do you agree?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Collective security is the idea that all states agree to act together against any state that commits aggression, so that peace is preserved by the threat of combined action. This was the principle of the League of Nations, founded in 1920 under the Covenant (Articles 10 and 16 provided for protection of members' territory and for sanctions). In the 1930s it failed to stop aggression in Manchuria (1931), Abyssinia (1935-36) and Europe. The statement attributes this largely to structural weaknesses of the League. The view is partly correct, but the decisive factor was the unwillingness of the leading members to use the League's powers, so that weak structure and weak will were closely connected.

**1. Structural weaknesses of the League.**
- *No armed force.* The League had no army of its own and depended on members to provide forces or to impose sanctions, which they were reluctant to do.
- *The unanimity rule.* Decisions of the Council and the Assembly normally required unanimity, so one member could block action and decisions were slow.
- *Incomplete membership.* The United States never joined, since the Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles in 1919-20; Germany was a member only from 1926 to 1933, Japan left in 1933 and Italy in 1937, while the Soviet Union was a member only from 1934 to 1939. Without the major powers, sanctions were weak: economic sanctions could not work without the participation of the United States.
- *Weak sanctions and procedures.* Economic sanctions depended on the cooperation of members, and the procedures of enquiry and delay were slow. The Covenant did not oblige members to take military action.
- *Dependence on Britain and France.* The League depended on the two powers, which were weakened by the Depression and by their own interests.

**2. Evidence from the 1930s.**
- *Manchuria (1931-33).* Japan invaded Manchuria in September 1931; the League sent the Lytton Commission, which condemned Japan in 1932, but no sanctions were applied and Japan simply left the League in 1933. The League was slow and powerless.
- *Abyssinia (1935-36).* Italy invaded Abyssinia in October 1935. The League imposed sanctions, but they excluded oil, coal and steel, and the Suez Canal remained open; Britain and France secretly negotiated the Hoare-Laval Pact (December 1935), and the League did nothing when Italy conquered the country in 1936. Haile Selassie's appeal to the League in 1936 was in vain.
- *Disarmament and Europe.* The Disarmament Conference (1932-34) failed; Germany left the League in 1933, rearmed, remilitarised the Rhineland in 1936 and annexed Austria in 1938, without League action.

**3. Other causes of ineffectiveness.**
- *National self-interest and lack of will.* Britain and France preferred to protect their own interests and avoid war, and followed appeasement. The "structural" weaknesses were therefore in part the result of this lack of will; the Covenant did allow sanctions, but the powers did not want to use them.
- *The Great Depression* (from 1929) made governments concentrate on domestic problems and reluctant to risk trade or rearmament; it also encouraged militarism in Japan, Italy and Germany.
- *The aggressive and determined dictators* (Japan, Mussolini, Hitler) were ready to ignore the League, and the Treaty of Versailles had created grievances that they exploited.
- *Public opinion in democracies* favoured peace and disarmament, and memories of the First World War made governments cautious.

**4. Evaluation.** Structural weaknesses were real and important, especially the lack of an armed force, the absence of major powers and the unanimity rule. But they were a symptom of the same underlying problem: the major powers were unwilling to sacrifice national interests for collective security. A stronger League would not have mattered without political will; and with political will, as the 1935 sanctions debate showed, the League could have acted more effectively (for example by banning oil).

**Conclusion.** I agree only partly. Structural defects made the League ineffective, but they were not the main cause of its failure. The more fundamental causes were the self-interest of Britain and France, the economic crisis and the determination of aggressive powers, which together prevented the League's structure from being used effectively.
